newsitem.title: GREECE: Salomon sees currency risk in Greek rate decline.
newsitem.headline: Salomon sees currency risk in Greek rate decline.

text.p: Salomon Brothers recommended an underweight position in Greek local currency assets and a neutral stance on Greek bonds, seeing currency risks by further falls in Greek interest rates.

"Historically low real yields and the slowdown of disinflation preclude a further significant fall in Greek interest rates without putting the authorities' exchange rate target at risk," Salomon said in its January debt strategy report.
Greece's still-high inflation differential with the EU and its deteriorating external position indicate that a fixed exchange rate policy may be difficult to maintain this year, it said.

And with Eurobond spreads at a 10-year low, the balance of risks favouring an increase in U.S. interest rates, further spread tightening appeared unlikely. Hence its neutral recommendation on Greek bonds.

It said that official projections of a pick up in GDP growth to 3.25 percent this year from an estimated 2.5 percent in 1996 may prove optimistic in view of the higher tax burden under the 1997 budget.

"The modest economic recovery has already prompted a deterioration in the external accounts. The deterioration reflects a rise in the trade deficit as well as lower tourist receipts and EU transfers," the report said.
On the inflation front, the government's targeted decline to 4.5 percent by end-1997 appeared ambitious.
Nevertheless, the withdrawal of fiscal stimulus under the 1997 budget and a drop in international oil prices could help reduce headline inflation to 6.5 percent by year-end 1997, it said.
The sustainability of the drachma exchange rate will depend on fiscal policy tightening.

"So far the authorities have followed an exchange rate-based disinflation strategy, with the rate of depreciation versus the ecu slowing from 10 percent in 1991 to approximate stability in 1996," Salomon said.
For 1997 monetary authorities will tolerate greater exchange rate volatility in order to discourage capital inflows by making day-to-day movements less predictable, it said.

Greece's 1997 budget target also appeared unattainable. Significant budgetary overruns in 1996 reduced the prospects for achieving this year's deficit target, putting at risk the country's objective of stabilising its public debt ratio.
Fiscal policy was being tightened but at a slower pace than required to meet EU convergence targets.
"In contrast to pre-election pledges, the government has imposed new taxes on real estate and on certain financial assets," Salomon said.
"It has abolished most tax exemptions to help achieve the ambitious 1997 deficit target of 4.2 percent of GDP, down from an estimated 7.6 percent in 1996," it added.
